query: For high-entropy alloys in demanding engineering applications, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention that could improve resistance to thermally induced toughness loss, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, defines the conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment that could falsify it?

generation.hypothesis: The addition of interstitial elements such as oxygen or nitrogen to a refractory high-entropy alloy can improve its resistance to thermally induced toughness loss by forming ordered interstitial complexes that impede dislocation motion and enhance strain hardening.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloy in its initial, unmodified state
generation.intervention: Addition of interstitial elements such as oxygen or nitrogen
generation.structural_mediator: Ordered interstitial complexes (OOCs/ONCs) formed by the added interstitial elements
generation.mechanism: Snoek relaxation and solid-solution strengthening due to the formation of OOCs/ONCs, which impede dislocation motion and enhance strain hardening
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved resistance to thermally induced toughness loss, as evidenced by increased yield strength, elongation, and damping capacity
generation.baseline: Unmodified refractory high-entropy alloy without added interstitial elements
generation.boundary: Temperature range of 300-1100 K, strain rates of 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ to 1 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹
generation.uncertainty: The exact nature and distribution of the ordered interstitial complexes, as well as their specific effects on dislocation motion and strain hardening, require further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the mechanical properties and microstructure of a refractory high-entropy alloy with and without added interstitial elements, using techniques such as tensile testing, damping measurements, and transmission electron microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of interstitial elements does not result in improved resistance to thermally induced toughness loss, as evidenced by no significant increase in yield strength, elongation, and damping capacity, then the hypothesis is falsified

System: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) synthesized from a blend of hydride powders (TiH2, ZrH2, HfH2, NbH, TaH0.5) and elemental powders. Processing: 3D ink-extrusion printing of inks containing hydride powders, de-binding under flowing H2 at 450 °C for 30 min, vacuum sintering at 1400 °C for 18 h, and silicide coating via pack cementation at 950 °C for 24 h. Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy alloys be designed to simultaneously achieve high Snoek-type damping capacity, high mechanical strength, and high ductility at elevated temperatures?. System: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi base HEA, (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 (O-2 HEA), and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98N2 (N-2 HEA). Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals (purity >99.9 wt%), TiN (99.9 wt%), and TiO2 (99.9 wt%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere; remelted at least eight times; drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold (10 mm × 10 mm × 60 mm). Test conditions: Damping measured via multifunction internal friction apparatus at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz, temperature range 300–1100 K, heating rate 2 K min⁻¹, max strain amplitude 2 × 10⁻⁴; Tensile tests at room temperature, strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹.
